procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 13, 1971 in Criminal Misc. Cases Nos. 169, 177, 222, 224, 229, 230, 231, 237, 285, 286, 287, 316, 328, 329, 330 and 331 of 1971.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court held that the Act in question was not a law made by Parliament in terms of Art. 22(7) of the Constitution. It further held that the provisions contained in ss. 11 and 13 of the Act relating to the procedure before the Advisory Board in respect of a person detained for a longer period than three months were ultra vires Art. 22(7) of the Constitution. The High Court concluded that Art. 19(1) was not applicable to the impugned Act and rejected the challenge based on Art. 14 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and set aside the judgment of the High Court. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to hear and dispose of the writ petitions on other points raised on the merits.

decision.appeal_result: Appeals are allowed and the judgment of the High Court is set aside.
directions: The writ petitions will now be heard and disposed of by the High Court on other points on the merits which require determination.

issue.issue_text: Whether Article 22(7) of the Constitution is mandatory, requiring Parliament to first enact a law prescribing the circumstances and procedure before a person can be detained for a period longer than three months.

facts: The High Court had previously ruled that a state law allowing detention for longer than three months was unconstitutional because Parliament had not first enacted a law under Article 22(7) of the Constitution.

The respondents argued that Article 22(7) makes it obligatory for Parliament to prescribe the maximum period of detention and the procedure for the Advisory Board before any person can be detained for more than three months.
law: Article 22(7) of the Constitution states that Parliament may by law prescribe the circumstances and classes of cases in which a person may be detained for a period longer than three months, the maximum period of detention, and the procedure to be followed by an Advisory Board.
application: The Supreme Court interpreted the plain language of Article 22(7), concluding that it merely "authorises or enables" Parliament to make such a law; it does not impose a "mandatory obligation" to do so.
The Court noted that even the counsel for the respondents conceded that the provision was enabling and permissive, not mandatory.

The Court reasoned that if the Constitution had intended for a Parliamentary law to be a prerequisite for any detention beyond three months, it would have included an express provision to that effect. The absence of such a provision was significant.

The Court characterized Parliament's power under Article 22(7) as an "overriding power," not an exclusive one. This means the absence of a law from Parliament does not prohibit a State Legislature from making its own law for preventive detention beyond three months, provided that law complies with the other constitutional safeguards, such as obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board as required by Article 22(4).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that Article 22(7) is not mandatory. It is an enabling or permissive provision that grants Parliament the power to legislate on the matter, but it does not require Parliament to enact a law as a precondition for a person to be detained for more than three months under a state law that otherwise complies with the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether a State Legislature is competent to make a law providing for preventive detention for more than three months, including prescribing the procedure for the Advisory Board, in the absence of a specific law on the subject by Parliament.

facts: A state law provided for preventive detention for a period longer than three months and also prescribed the procedure for the Advisory Board.
The High Court had found these provisions to be invalid, holding that only Parliament had the jurisdiction to legislate on these matters under Article 22(7) of the Constitution.

law.name: Article 246 & List III, Entry 3 of the Seventh Schedule
law.description: Grants concurrent powers to both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws regarding "preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State, the maintenance of public order, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community."

law.name: Article 22(4) of the Constitution
law.description: Prohibits any law from authorizing detention for more than three months unless an Advisory Board has reported, before the three months expire, that there is sufficient cause for such detention.

law.name: Article 22(7) of the Constitution
law.description: States that Parliament *may* by law prescribe the circumstances for detention beyond three months without an Advisory Board's opinion, the maximum period of detention, and the procedure for the Advisory Board.

application.point: State's Power is Concurrent, Not Subordinate
application.explanation: The Court established that under Article 246 and Entry 3 of List III, State Legislatures have plenary and co-extensive power with Parliament to legislate on preventive detention. This power is subject only to the condition that the state law does not conflict with a law made by Parliament on the same matter.

The Court rejected the argument that Article 22(7) grants exclusive jurisdiction to Parliament. It held that the word "may" in the article signifies a permissive or overriding power, not a mandatory or exclusive one. This means Parliament is *enabled* to make a law on these specific aspects, but its failure to do so does not create a bar on the State Legislature.

application.point: Absence of Parliamentary Law is Not a Limitation
application.explanation: The Court reasoned that the absence of a law made by Parliament under Article 22(7) does not limit the State Legislature's power. A State can still enact a law for detention beyond three months, provided it complies with the general safeguard in Article 22(4)(a), which requires a positive opinion from an Advisory Board. The Court noted that if the Constitution had intended to make the State's power conditional on a prior Parliamentary law, it would have stated so explicitly.

application.point: State Can Legislate on Advisory Board Procedure
application.explanation: Since the power to legislate on preventive detention is concurrent, it necessarily includes the power to legislate on incidental matters, such as the procedure to be followed by the Advisory Board. Therefore, a State Legislature is competent to prescribe this procedure in its own preventive detention law, as long as it does not conflict with a central law.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument that a State Legislature is competent to make a law providing for preventive detention for more than three months and to prescribe the procedure for the Advisory Board. The Court held that the State's power is concurrent with Parliament's and is not dependent on a specific law being enacted by Parliament on the subject. The absence of a Parliamentary law under the permissive powers of Article 22(7) does not invalidate a State law that otherwise complies with the constitutional requirements of Article 22(4).

issue.issue_text: Whether the challenge to the general vires of the Act was valid.

facts: A challenge was made against the general validity (vires) of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
The argument was that the restrictions imposed by the Act on citizens' freedoms were not in the interest of the general public.
law: Restrictions on a citizen's freedom, such as those under Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution, can be justified if they are in the interest of the general public.
A court can take judicial notice of historical events to understand the context and necessity of a law.
application: The Supreme Court took judicial notice of the historical events in West Bengal that led to the imposition of President's rule.
The Court found that these events fully demonstrated the necessity of the Act in the interest of the general public.
Consequently, the restrictions placed by the Act on citizens' freedom were held to be "eminently in the interest of the general public."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, finding that the general argument against the vires of the Act was "wholly without substance" because the law was necessary in the interest of the general public given the historical context.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in holding that sections 11 and 13 of the Act were ultra vires Article 22(7) of the Constitution.

facts: The High Court had ruled that sections 11 and 13 of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, were unconstitutional.
law: The High Court's reasoning was that Article 22(7) of the Constitution grants Parliament the exclusive power to legislate on matters concerning detention for a period longer than three months and the procedure to be followed by an Advisory Board.
Based on this interpretation, the High Court concluded that the State Legislature was incompetent to make such a law.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's interpretation of Article 22(7).
It held that Article 22(7) is not mandatory but permissive.

The Court explained that the article "merely authorises or enables" Parliament to make a law on these specific aspects of preventive detention; it does not prohibit a State Legislature from legislating on the same subject.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, finding that because Article 22(7) is permissive and not an exclusive grant of power to Parliament, sections 11 and 13 of the Act were valid and not unconstitutional.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Article 22(7) of the Constitution is mandatory, requiring Parliament to first enact a law prescribing the circumstances and procedure before a person can be detained for a period longer than three months.
appellant_arguments: Article 22(7) of the Constitution does not confer exclusive jurisdiction on Parliament to make a law for detention longer than three months, implying it is not a mandatory precondition for a state law.
respondent_arguments: The word 'may' in the opening part of Article 22(7) must be read as 'shall', making it a mandatory duty for Parliament to enact such a law before a state can legislate on the matter.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a State Legislature is competent to make a law providing for preventive detention for more than three months, including prescribing the procedure for the Advisory Board, in the absence of a specific law on the subject by Parliament.
appellant_arguments: The State Legislature is fully competent to make laws for detention, to prescribe the procedure for the Advisory Board, and to legislate for detention beyond the period of three months.
respondent_arguments: A State Legislature is not competent to make such a law in the absence of a law by Parliament under Article 22(7), as that is a mandatory precondition.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the challenge to the general vires of the Act was valid.
appellant_arguments: The challenge to the general vires of the Act is wholly without substance.
respondent_arguments: The respondents challenged the general vires of the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in holding that sections 11 and 13 of the Act were ultra vires Article 22(7) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's judgment was incorrect; the sections are not ultra vires.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was correct in its finding that the sections were ultra vires Article 22(7).

cases.case_name: S. Krishnan v. State of Madras
cases.principle: The case was relied on to dismiss the general argument challenging the vires (constitutional validity) of the Act.
The case was relied on to dismiss the general argument challenging the vires (constitutional validity) of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: There is a fairly close and rational nexus between the clauses of an Act and the maintenance of public order and security of the State.
obiter: The Court can and should take judicial notice of historical events.
The restrictions placed by the Act must be held to be eminently in the interest of the general public.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The challenge to the general vires of the Act is without substance because the restrictions it places on citizen's freedom are in the interest of the general public. The historical events leading to the President's rule, of which the court can take judicial notice, fully demonstrate the necessity for the Act. A potentially overbroad provision concerning insults to objects of public veneration can be constitutionally validated by construing it narrowly to apply only to acts done in public view that are capable of arousing indignation and thus disturbing public order.
legal_tests_applied: Rational Nexus Test: The court assessed whether there was a 'fairly close and rational nexus' between the clauses of the Act and the maintenance of public order and security of the State.

Judicial Notice of Historical Context: The court determined it 'can and should take judicial notice of the historic'1 l events which led to the President's rule' to evaluate the necessity of the law in the interest of the general public.

Principle of Narrow Construction (Reading Down): To save a provision from being unconstitutional, the court applied a restrictive construction, 'legitimately imputing to the law-maker the intention to enact a valid provision of law within the constitutional limitations designed effectively to achieve its object and purpose.'
policy_considerations: Security of a State, maintenance of public order, and of supplies and services essential to the community demand effective safeguards in the larger interest of sustenance of peaceful democratic way of life.
The necessity of the Act was demonstrated by the historical events that led to the imposition of President's rule in the state, which the court took into account.
